b1.note: True as worded, but the mechanism is more specific: the page must be a secure context and serve Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin plus Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp (COEP: credentialless is an accepted alternative that avoids requiring CORP on every subresource); crossOriginIsolated then reads true. Chrome historically allowed non-COI SharedArrayBuffer for a period and ran a deprecation/reverse-origin trial before full enforcement (Chrome 92+ enforcement, trial concluded around Chrome 106); nothing since then has removed the COI gate. In a cross-origin iframe the 'cross-origin-isolated' permissions policy (default allowlist 'self') also has to be granted by the embedder.

b2.note: timestamp-query shipped enabled-by-default on desktop Chromium (Chrome 121 timeframe) after a long period gated behind enable-unsafe-webgpu, but with deliberately reduced precision (timestamps quantized to ~100 us) as a Spectre/timing-side-channel mitigation, and some configurations/OS builds have regated it. Because my knowledge is ~mid-2025 and I have no live source, treat 'default-on' as unverified for 2026; check webgpureport.org in the target build.

b3.verdict: disagree: WASM module validation succeeds without cross-origin isolation; the failure happens later, at instantiation (constructing/compiling a shared WebAssembly.Memory, { shared:true }), which throws a RuntimeError/LinkError when the document is not cross-origin isolated
b3.note: WebAssembly.validate is a purely syntactic/type check and has no COI dependency. The COI dependency lives in SharedArrayBuffer/WebAssembly.Memory shared:true creation, which is why threads-capable modules (and any toolchain output using shared memory or pthreads) fail at instantiate/compile time, not at validate time, in Chrome, Firefox and Safari alike.

rows.claim: SharedArrayBuffer is exposed only in a secure context whose document is cross-origin isolated: COOP: same-origin AND COEP: require-corp (or COEP: credentialless) on the document itself, giving crossOriginIsolated === true; Chrome 92+ enforced this after the non-COI deprecation/reverse-origin trial ended (~Chrome 106). Edge (Chromium) behaves identically.

rows.claim: A cross-origin iframe can be cross-origin isolated, but only if (a) it serves its own COOP: same-origin + COEP: require-corp/credentialless, (b) its ancestor chain is also cross-origin isolated, and (c) the embedder grants the 'cross-origin-isolated' permissions policy on the iframe element (allow="cross-origin-isolated"), since that feature's default allowlist is 'self'. WebGPU itself is not COI-gated (secure context + GPU availability only), so a non-COI iframe can still get a GPUDevice, but without SharedArrayBuffer/wasm threads and with reduced timestamp precision.
rows.verifier_hint: HTML spec 'cross-origin isolated capability' + Permissions Policy 'cross-origin-isolated'; web.dev COOP/COEP guide; webgpureport.org inside an iframe
rows.notes: Mechanically the hardest cell in the grid: three independent conditions and a permissions-policy gate. Deployment implication: if your prover is embedded (e.g., in a wallet or dapp page), you usually cannot self-grant COI — the embedder must opt in.
